title: Aural Architecture as Affect: Understanding the Impact of Acoustic Environments on Human Experience
research_question:
1. How does the acoustic environment influence human experience and impact emotions?
2. What are the acoustic characteristics and parameters related to that emotional impact?
3. What are the links between the acoustic characteristics and the emotional impact?

participants.description: 9 males and 11 females from diverse cultural backgrounds (religious affiliation, nationalities) aged between 20 and 40 years old.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but study was approved by the authors’ institution Review Board.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Virtual reality environment recreating 360-degree visuals and 3D sounds of built worship spaces.
Binaural recordings of dry Quran recitations (for mosques) and Christian hymns (for churches), and wet recordings captured in four worship spaces. Each stimulus was ±75 seconds long.
360-degree visuals of the buildings’ interiors collected using Samsung Gear 360 4K camera. Visuals were identical for dry and wet recordings of the same building.

measures.instrument: Selection of keywords (sad, tense, nostalgic, spiritual, inspired, cheerful, thrilled)
Self-report rating scale (1: Not familiar, 3: Very familiar)
Photoplethysmography (PPG) sensor (E4-Empatica wristband), 1 Hz sampling rate
Electrodermal activity (EDA) sensor (E4-Empatica wristband), 4 Hz sampling rate
ITA MATLAB Toolbox (calculated from Impulse Response)
Calculated from G Low and G Mid
Calculated from T30 at low and mid frequencies
Calculated from frequency (f) and T30 (Q(f)= 0.227 x f x T30)

findings.antecedent: Familiarity with religious recording content ('very familiar' vs. 'unfamiliar')
findings.mechanism: Cultural background and prior experience amplify physiological response, possibly due to high arousal emotions like excitement or tension from unfamiliarity.
findings.quote: participants who reported being very familiar with the recording content responded with a heart rate median that was ±10 points higher than that of the group who reported being unfamiliar.

findings.antecedent: Familiarity with worship spaces/acoustic environment ('never/rarely visited' vs. 'occasionally visited')
findings.mechanism: Cultural background and prior experience amplify physiological response.
findings.quote: participants who reported they never or rarely visited a similar religious space responded with a heart rate that was higher than in those who occasionally visited, by ±4 points.

findings.antecedent: Dry recordings (absence of acoustic environment influence)
findings.consequent: Auditory experience (flat, inside the head, too close, intimate, uncomfortable, focus on musicality/performance errors, unreal, disconnected from visual, coming from loudspeaker, doesn't fit space)

findings.quote: participants described their experience during listening to the dry recordings as unreal, in addition to mentioning the disconnection between audio and visuals.

findings.consequent: Auditory experience (echoey, amplified, harmonized, surrounding, hard to localize, spacious, immersive, sense of belonging, inviting to participate)
findings.mechanism: Acoustic reflections create a sense of envelopment and immersion, enhancing the experience.
findings.quote: when they listened to the wet recordings, they described the sound as surrounding them, which made it hard to localize the sound source, as it seemed to be coming from everywhere.

findings.antecedent: Wet recording of A2 (rectangular plan, flat low ceiling) vs. cultural expectations of a grand mosque
findings.consequent: Perceived fit with visuals/cultural expectations (felt fake, sound didn't match space)
findings.mechanism: Mismatch between expected acoustic environment (based on visual cues of grand mosque) and actual acoustics creates discomfort/unreality.
findings.quote: some mentioned that the wet recording of A2 did not fit in with the visuals and felt fake. They explained that the interior of A2 does not represent what that they would expect a mosque to look like

findings.antecedent: Repeated convolution of Impulse Response (IR) with sound source
findings.consequent: Visual distinguishability of amplified frequencies (room modes)
findings.mechanism: Iterative process amplifies resonant frequencies, making them more prominent in the spectrum.
findings.quote: Those peaks and dips become more distinguishable when the convolution is repeated multiple times

findings.antecedent: Sound source type (vocal vs. cello) in Room 1
findings.mechanism: Room modes interact with the dominant frequencies of the sound source, leading to selective amplification.
findings.quote: the spectrum shows different peaks resulted from the room modes and the dominant frequencies of the sound source.

findings.antecedent: Room geometry (base case Room 1 vs modified Room 2)
findings.consequent: Amplification level at 100-1000 Hz (using sound source 1)
findings.mechanism: Changes in room geometry alter the impulse response and thus the frequency-domain response.
findings.quote: room 2 has a lower amplitude by ±3 dB at the frequency range 100–1000 Hz.

findings.antecedent: Room geometry (base case Room 1 vs modified Room 2) with multiple convolutions (sound source 1)
findings.consequent: Visual distinguishability of individual modes at low frequencies (<100 Hz)
findings.mechanism: Multiple convolutions enhance the visibility of room modes, especially in complex geometries.
findings.quote: The individual modes at low frequencies <100 Hz in (room 2) became more visually identifiable

findings.mechanism: Absorptive materials reduce reflections and sound level.
findings.quote: using highly absorptive materials caused the sound level to decrease

findings.mechanism: Reflective materials enhance sound reflections and amplification.
findings.quote: the room with reflective surfaces caused an amplification of the sound level—especially at low frequencies

findings.antecedent: Room modes identified by AMROC calculator
findings.consequent: Room modes identified by multiple convolution method
findings.quote: The results of the room modes obtained by the AMROC room mode calculator (Fig. 3.17; top) and the room modes identified by the developed multiple convolution method are in good agreement

findings.antecedent: Adding absorptive panels to room walls
findings.mechanism: Absorbers reduce sound reflections, particularly at higher frequencies.
findings.quote: adding absorbers reduced the amplification at high frequencies above 1000 Hz

findings.antecedent: Adding absorptive panels to room walls
findings.mechanism: Absorbers can shift the balance of amplification, sometimes increasing low frequencies.
findings.quote: increased it at low frequencies below 100 Hz.

findings.mechanism: The room's geometry and materials cause specific frequency bands to be amplified.
findings.quote: In all locations, the frequency band that was amplified the most was similar (100–500 Hz—the dominant frequency range of the sound source).

findings.mechanism: High frequency modes are more susceptible to changes in source/receiver location.
findings.quote: modes at high frequencies were more sensitive to location, which is evident in the results of the multiple convolutions

findings.antecedent: Longer reverberation time (T30) at 250 Hz in DCA
findings.mechanism: Reverberation time is positively correlated with resonance quality, leading to greater amplification of frequencies within the dominant band of the sound source.
findings.quote: Since reverberation time is positively correlated with resonance quality (Heller, 2013), and since 250 Hz falls within the dominant frequency band of the sound source, the latter was amplified more

findings.consequent: Early Decay Time (EDT) at frequencies <1000 Hz
findings.quote: all the buildings (except A2) have longer EDT at frequencies <1000 Hz.

findings.mechanism: Longer reverberation times at low frequencies are preferred in choral music.
findings.quote: reverberation time for all the buildings (except A2) follows the same pattern in having the longest T30 values (2–3 seconds) between 250 Hz and 1000 Hz

findings.mechanism: Lower C80 at low frequencies contributes to aesthetics, while higher C80 at mid/high frequencies preserves speech intelligibility.
findings.quote: A1 had the highest contrast, with the lowest C80 values at frequencies <1000 Hz and the highest values >1000 Hz.

findings.mechanism: Lower C80 at low frequencies contributes to aesthetics, while higher C80 at mid/high frequencies preserves speech intelligibility.
findings.quote: A1 had the highest contrast, with the lowest C80 values at frequencies <1000 Hz and the highest values >1000 Hz.

findings.mechanism: Higher absorption at mid frequencies (e.g., carpet flooring) can lead to higher bass gain.
findings.quote: A1 showed the highest G Bass value

findings.mechanism: Higher BR is associated with sound amplification of male voice frequencies and added warmth.
findings.quote: A1 has the highest BR.

findings.mechanism: Larger volumes may be associated with less emotional arousal due to extensively long reverberation time.
findings.quote: The result of the Pearson correlation analysis between volume and emotional response showed a negative correlation with HRR (-0.99, p-value < .01)

findings.mechanism: Larger volumes may be associated with less emotional arousal.
findings.quote: and EDR (-0.45, p-value < .05).

findings.mechanism: Low frequencies (125 Hz) are within the human vocal range and can be amplified by room resonance, enhancing spiritual emotions.
findings.quote: At 125 Hz, G had a significant correlation with SRR (p-value < .01).

findings.mechanism: EDT at low frequencies may influence physiological arousal.
findings.quote: EDT and T30 had significant correlation with HRR and SRR respectively (p-value < .05).

findings.mechanism: Longer reverberation at low frequencies can enhance the perceived spiritual quality of the sound.
findings.quote: EDT and T30 had significant correlation with HRR and SRR respectively (p-value < .05).

findings.mechanism: Sound strength at low-mid frequencies contributes to the emotional impact.
findings.quote: At 250 Hz, G had a significant correlation with SRR (p-value < .01).

findings.mechanism: Reverberation time at mid-frequencies may influence physiological arousal.
findings.quote: At 1000 Hz, T30 had a significant correlation with HRR (p-value < .05).

findings.mechanism: EDT at high frequencies may influence physiological arousal.
findings.quote: At 8000 Hz, EDT had significant correlation with EDR (p-value < .05)

findings.mechanism: Sound strength at high frequencies may influence physiological arousal.
findings.quote: G had significant correlation with HRR (p-value < .05).

findings.mechanism: Bass gain contributes to the richness and warmth of sound, enhancing spiritual emotions.
findings.quote: the Pearson correlation between G Bass and SSR was 0.82 (p-value < .01)

findings.antecedent: Islamic Center of America (A1) impulse response
findings.mechanism: Architectural features of A1 lead to higher amplification at low frequencies.
findings.quote: A1 has the highest magnitude at frequencies <200 Hz compared to the other buildings.

findings.antecedent: Islamic Center of America (A1) and Islamic Center of Detroit (A2) impulse responses
findings.mechanism: Specific architectural features create distinct room modes at certain frequencies.
findings.quote: A1 and A2 have strong individual modes at 108, 123 Hz for A1 and 120 Hz for A2, with magnitude levels that are 10–15 dB higher than the neighboring frequencies.

findings.mechanism: A2's acoustic characteristics result in lower resonance quality at low frequencies.
findings.quote: A2 has the smallest Q valueS below 1000 Hz.

findings.mechanism: A1's acoustic characteristics result in higher resonance quality at 125 Hz.
findings.quote: at 125 Hz, A1 has the largest Q value

findings.mechanism: A1's acoustic characteristics result in a smaller resonance width at 125 Hz.
findings.quote: A1 has the smallest width (3.45 Hz)

findings.mechanism: A2's smaller volume contributes to a larger resonance width.
findings.quote: A2 has the largest (25 Hz)

findings.antecedent: Auralization of A1 vs A2 (using sound source 1)
findings.mechanism: Different architectural characteristics lead to different frequency amplification patterns.
findings.quote: A1 reinforced the low and mid frequencies, which are the dominant ones of the sound source, and given that A1 was rated significantly higher for the emotional impact (spiritual) than A2

findings.consequent: Visual distinguishability of dominant frequencies reinforced by room
findings.mechanism: Repeating the convolution makes the amplified frequencies more visually evident.
findings.quote: The multiple auralization makes it visually easier to distinguish the dominant frequencies reinforced by the room.

findings.antecedent: Auralizations of studied buildings (repeated four times)
findings.consequent: Peak in frequency domain at 125 Hz
findings.mechanism: The method effectively identifies room modes and their reinforcement of dominant frequencies.
findings.quote: The graphs show a peak at 125 Hz in all buildings except B2, with A1 showing the highest peak.

findings.mechanism: The auralization algorithm may not realistically represent low frequencies.
findings.quote: the auralization results show a significant drop in the magnitude value at frequencies <200 Hz.

findings.antecedent: High Bass Ratio (BR) and lower resonance width
findings.mechanism: These acoustic characteristics contribute to a more desirable auditory experience, enhancing emotional impact.
findings.quote: the buildings with the highest BR and lower resonance width received a higher rating for emotional impact.

findings.mechanism: Resonance quality contributes to the perceived richness and emotional depth of the acoustic environment.
findings.quote: resonance width is inversely related to resonance quality, this also indicates that the buildings with higher resonance quality resulted in higher emotional impact.

mechanisms: Acoustic environment amplifies sound, enriching it in frequency and time domains, creating harmonized sound and enhancing emotional effect.
Reverberation increases perceived size, provides dramatic effect, and destroys localization cues, creating a sense of mystery.
Sound harmonization by blending musical notes influences emotions.
Resonance (room modes) amplifies specific frequency bands, which can provoke emotional responses.
Cultural background and familiarity influence the interpretation of acoustic stimuli and amplify emotional impact.
Mismatch between visual and aural cues (e.g., grand visuals with dry sound) creates discomfort.
Low frequencies (e.g., 125 Hz) are within the human vocal range and can be reinforced by room resonance, enhancing spiritual emotions.
Sound strength (G) highly impacts the perception of loudness at low frequencies.
Nonuniform amplification across frequency bands in real spaces (due to natural reverberation) differs from artificial reverberation, potentially impacting emotions.
moderators: Cultural background (familiarity with sound and acoustic environment)
Sound source characteristics (frequency content, type of music/chant)
implementation_implications: Architects should consider aural aspects in designing buildings, especially when sound is integral to activities.
Design guidelines should be developed based on acoustic requirements that support spiritual experience, moving beyond replicating historic designs.
Understanding the contribution of architectural features in reinforcing different frequency ranges can lead to better acoustic environments and sound illusions.

The developed auralization method can be used as a diagnostic tool for evaluating existing rooms and informing design decisions for modifying geometry, volume, and materials to achieve desired acoustic amplification.
Caution should be exercised when using auralization for subjective evaluation of worship spaces, as low frequencies might not be represented realistically.

Future research should explore architectural features that reinforce low frequencies to enhance spiritual emotions and provide design guidelines based on space activity and required frequency enhancement.
Multisensory VR representations can be used for cultural heritage preservation and architectural acoustics education.
Further research is needed to identify architectural features effective in enhancing positive affect and to develop tools for designing supportive acoustic environments with restorative qualities.

limitations: Some results are specific to worship spaces and may not generalize to other types of emotions or spaces.
The study used binaural recording which does not account for head movement, potentially limiting realism.
The multiple convolution method in simulation provides a general band for room modes, not absolute modes, and its realism for low frequencies in auralization is a concern.

paper_metadata.title: Factors Affecting Auditory Estimates of Virtual Room Size: Effects of Stimulus, Level, and Reverberation
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Factors Affecting Auditory Estimates of Virtual Room Size: Effects of Stimulus, Level, and Reverberation
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: When vision is unavailable, auditory level and reverberation cues provide important spatial information regarding the environment, such as the size of a room. We investigated how room-size estimates were affected by stimulus type, level, and reverberation. In Experiment 1, 15 blindfolded participants estimated room size after performing a distance bisection task in virtual rooms that were either anechoic (with level cues only) or reverberant (with level and reverberation cues) with a relatively short reverberation time of T60 = 400 milliseconds. Speech, noise, or clicks were presented at distances between 1.9 and 7.1 m. The reverberant room was judged to be significantly larger than the anechoic room ( p <  .05) for all stimuli. In Experiment 2, only the reverberant room was used and the overall level of all sounds was equalized, so only reverberation cues were available. Ten blindfolded participants took part. Room-size estimates were significantly larger for speech than for clicks or noise. The results show that when level and reverberation cues are present, reverberation increases judged room size. Even relatively weak reverberation cues provide room-size information, which could potentially be used by blind or visually impaired individuals encountering novel rooms.
